performed_via_github_app.description:
Publish incredibly high performance websites and applications right from GitHub. The Netlify platform connects your repositories to an all-in-one workflow for global CDN deployment, continuous integration, and automatic (and free) HTTPS. Each time you commit changes, Netlify builds your site, prerenders markup, and optimizes assets on dedicated build infrastructure. Easily create an entirely automated workflows for your web applications

## Features

### Push your site live, directly from GitHub
Deploy your site to an ultra-redundant global CDN that’s purpose built for serving pages and assets quickly and consistently.

### Automate deployment
Netlify’s built-in Continuous Deployment automatically runs your build commands and deploys the result whenever you push to your Git repository.

### Add a custom domain
Purchase domains and manage DNS zones and records right inside of Netlify.

### HTTPS is automatic
Your site will automatically be secured with a free TLS certificate from Let’s Encrypt.

### Deploy Previews
Netlify’s Deploy Previews streamlined your workflow by giving you a unique, permanent URL to check what your changes will be like in production whenever you submit a pull request.

### And a lot more!
Netlify includes solutions for forms, identity, and even custom functions powered by AWS Lambda. And all this functionality can be configured directly in your repo.

body:
## Review (Claude Fable 5): base-ui#4980 — [drawer] Drive swipe gestures natively

This routes drawer swipe moves through the existing document-level capture-phase `touchmove` listener: once the drawer claims the gesture it calls `stopPropagation()` and forwards the event into `useSwipeDismiss` via the new `moveNative` method, so the move never reaches React's delegated touch system — which was what triggered ~2 paints per move. The drag transform also moves to `translate3d`, and the old React `onTouchMove` plumbing in `DrawerViewport` is removed.

**Correctness** — traced the forwarding path end to end:

- The synthetic object passed to `handleMove` supplies exactly the five fields the move pipeline reads (`touches`, `currentTarget`, `nativeEvent`, `defaultPrevented`, `timeStamp`); `getPrimaryPointerPosition` and `isTouchLikeEvent` branch on `'touches' in event`, so the native shape flows through the touch path identically to a React event. The `defaultPrevented` snapshot (vs. React's live getter) is only read on the non-touch branch, so freezing it is harmless.
- `currentTarget` is the same element the React touch props were spread onto (`viewportElement ?? popupElement`), so the scrollable-boundary check in `handleMoveCore` is unchanged.
- Propagation is preserved everywhere the drawer must not hijack the gesture: range inputs, two-finger pinch, text selection, cross-axis native scroll, and in-progress scrolling of inner containers. The old React-side guard (`allowSwipe === false || (scrollTarget != null && !allowSwipe)`) maps cleanly onto the new branches — forward only when `scrollTarget` is null/doc/body, or when `allowSwipe === true`.
- One theoretical gap: the doc/body branch forwards without re-checking `allowSwipe === false`, where the old guard would have skipped. In practice it's unreachable — native touch events keep targeting the touchstart element, so a gesture that began on a range input never reaches that branch (and a touchstart on a range input nulls out `touchState` entirely).

**Notes:**

1. **Observable behavior change.** User-attached React `onTouchMove` handlers inside the drawer no longer fire while the drawer owns the gesture (the new test asserts this). That's the point of the fix, but it's API-observable — worth a line in the changelog for anyone reading swipe moves themselves. `onTouchStart`/`onTouchEnd` still fire, so consumers see start → end with no moves in between.
2. The "non-overflowing scroll container" branch stops propagation without forwarding to the swipe — consistent, since `preventDefault` already made the gesture inert there; just noting it's the one spot where propagation stops without the swipe consuming the move.
3. The hook method is named `moveNative` and documented in terms of the mechanism (capture-phase consumers claiming the gesture) rather than the Drawer specifically, keeping the shared util component-agnostic — Toast also consumes it. Since the property key survives minification, the short name also saves a few bundle bytes.

**Tests** cover both the claimed path (consumer handler not called) and the preserved native-scroll path (handler called once), and the `translate3d` assertion tolerates browser serialization differences. Benchmark methodology in the description is appropriately honest about cross-library caveats.

LGTM — the notes above are observations, not blockers.
